\chapter{Bringing, Getting, Waiting, Buying}
\label{ch:pt-bringing-getting-waiting-buying}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I bring, get, wait for and buy in Portuguese, use conseguir for managing to do a thing, let esperar carry waiting, hoping and expecting at once, and tell comprar's Latin root from the identically spelled one behind English compare.}

The chapter's last lesson closes the set: after comprar the reader produces all four first-person forms in one run - trago, consigo, espero, compro - separates the comparare that gave comprar (com- + parare, 'to procure') from the identically spelled comparare that gave English compare (com- + par, 'equal'), and re-reads tenho comprado as 'I have been buying', not 'I have bought'.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[trazer]{trazer — bringing, and the dragging behind it}

\label{lesson:PT-C21-trazer}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter split English \textquotedblleft{}take\textquotedblright{} in two. Here is a third kind of handling: not grabbing a thing, not consuming it, but carrying it toward you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Two forms to learn whole}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{trago} & nós \textbf{trazemos} \\
tu \textbf{trazes} & vocês/eles \textbf{trazem} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{traz} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Trazer} is \textquotedblleft{}to bring\textquotedblright{} — to carry something toward the speaker. Two forms cannot be worked out. The \emph{eu} form is \textbf{trago}, with a hard \emph{g} no other form has, and the \emph{ele} form is bare \textbf{traz}, with nothing after the \emph{z}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Trago o pão.} — \textquotedblleft{}I bring the bread.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Gosto de trazer o vinho.} — \textquotedblleft{}I like to bring the wine.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

That second sentence keeps \emph{gostar} welded to its \textbf{de}: \emph{gosto de} and then a verb, never \emph{gosto} alone. The past of \emph{trazer} is \textbf{trouxe}, \textquotedblleft{}I brought\textquotedblright{} — irregular, and learned as one whole word.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{trazer} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{trahere}}, \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{drag}, to pull,\textquotedblright{} which reached Portuguese through a worn-down \emph{tragere}. To bring a thing was first of all to haul it.

English owns the family, nearly all of it through \emph{tractus}, \textquotedblleft{}dragged\textquotedblright{}: a \textbf{tractor} drags, \textbf{traction} is the grip that pulls, you \textbf{attract} by drawing toward, \textbf{subtract} by drawing away, \textbf{extract} by drawing out, and you are \textbf{distracted} when attention is drawn apart. A \textbf{contract} draws parties together; something \textbf{abstract} has been drawn off the thing itself.

Set that beside the last chapter's two takings. \textbf{Pegar} came from \emph{picāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to coat with pitch,\textquotedblright{} so a thing sticks to your hand; \textbf{tomar} has no settled Latin root at all. Three verbs of handling — and only \emph{trazer} has travel in it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}trago, trazes, traz, trazemos, trazem\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Trago o pão\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Trouxe o pão\textquotedblright{}
  \item liking, once a tasting — \textquotedblleft{}Gosto de trazer o vinho\textquotedblright{}
  \item grabbing, consuming, carrying — \textquotedblleft{}pego · tomo · trago\textquotedblright{}
  \item the dragging family — \textquotedblleft{}tractor · attract · subtract\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{trazer}. (\textbf{Trago, trazes, traz, trazemos, trazem}.) Which two forms were learned whole? (\textbf{Trago}, with its \emph{g}, and bare \textbf{traz}.) What did \emph{trahere} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{drag}\textquotedblright{} — so a \emph{tractor} pulls.) Which small word does \emph{gostar} keep before a verb, and what did its root \emph{gustāre} mean? (\emph{\textbf{De}}; \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{taste}\textquotedblright{}.) Which verb of taking came from \textquotedblleft{}to coat with pitch,\textquotedblright{} and which has no settled root at all? (\emph{\textbf{Pegar}}, from \emph{picāre}; \emph{\textbf{tomar}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[conseguir / obter]{conseguir / obter — getting, and managing to}

\label{lesson:PT-C21-conseguir}



\begin{quote}
English \textquotedblleft{}get\textquotedblright{} is one of the vaguest verbs it owns. Portuguese answers it with a verb that also does a job English needs a whole phrase for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Get a thing, or manage a deed}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{consigo} & nós \textbf{conseguimos} \\
tu \textbf{consegues} & vocês/eles \textbf{conseguem} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{consegue} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Watch the \emph{eu} form: the stem's \emph{e} becomes an \textbf{i} in \textbf{consigo}, and nowhere else.

\emph{Conseguir} has two jobs. With a noun it is \textbf{to get, to obtain}. With another verb straight after it, it is \textbf{to manage to, to succeed in} — the sense English has no single word for:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Consigo trazer o pão.} — \textquotedblleft{}I can manage to bring the bread.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Consigo ajudar.} — \textquotedblleft{}I manage to help.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Its formal twin is \textbf{obter}, which belongs to paperwork rather than speech — and which you can already conjugate, because it is \emph{ter} with \textbf{ob-} bolted on: \textbf{obtenho}, \textbf{obtém}, exactly as \textbf{tenho}, \textbf{tem}.

The polite address from the opening chapters still works: to a stranger, \textbf{o senhor consegue trazer o pão}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{conseguir} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{cōnsequī}}, \textquotedblleft{}to follow right through to the end,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{con-} (\textquotedblleft{}all the way\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{\textbf{sequī}}, \textquotedblleft{}to follow.\textquotedblright{} To \emph{conseguir} is to have followed a thing to where it stops — which is why one verb covers both getting the object and pulling the deed off.

English took \emph{sequī} everywhere: a \textbf{sequel} follows, a \textbf{sequence} is things in following order, a \textbf{consequence} is what follows from, and \textbf{pursue} is the same verb through French. Best of all, \textbf{second} is \emph{secundus}, \textquotedblleft{}the following one\textquotedblright{} — a number whose name means \textquotedblleft{}next.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{obter} $\leftarrow$ \emph{\textbf{obtinēre}}, whose \emph{tinēre} is \emph{tenēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to hold\textquotedblright{} — the very verb behind \textbf{ter}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}consigo, consegues, consegue, conseguimos, conseguem\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Consigo trazer o pão\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Consigo ajudar\textquotedblright{}
  \item holding and getting — \textquotedblleft{}tenho · obtenho\textquotedblright{}
  \item politely — \textquotedblleft{}O senhor consegue trazer o pão?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the following family — \textquotedblleft{}sequel · sequence · second\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I manage to help\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I bring the bread.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Consigo ajudar}}; \emph{\textbf{trago o pão}}.) What did \emph{sequī} mean, and which number is named from it? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{follow}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{\textbf{second}}, \emph{secundus}.) Which verb is \emph{obter} built on, and what did that root mean? (\emph{\textbf{Ter}}, from \emph{tenēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{hold}\textquotedblright{}.) Which verb came from \emph{adiūtāre}, its \emph{i} hardening into a \emph{j}? (\emph{\textbf{Ajudar}}.) And the polite address for a stranger? (\emph{\textbf{O senhor}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[esperar]{esperar — to wait}

\label{lesson:PT-C21-esperar}



\begin{quote}
One ordinary \textbf{-ar} verb lets you say that you wait: \textbf{esperar}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The present tense}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{espero} & nós \textbf{esperamos} \\
tu \textbf{esperas} & vocês/eles \textbf{esperam} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{espera} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The endings are familiar. Portuguese normally puts the thing or person waited for directly after the verb:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Espero o meu irmão.} — I am waiting for my brother.
\end{quote}

English needs “for”; Portuguese does not add a preposition here.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Esperar} comes from Latin \emph{\textbf{spērāre}}, “to hope.” Its front \textbf{e-} props up an older \emph{sp-} beginning, just as \textbf{escrever} grew from Latin \emph{scrībere}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{espero, esperas, espera, esperamos, esperam}
  \item “I am waiting for my brother” — \textbf{Espero o meu irmão.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say “I wait.” (\textbf{Espero.}) Say “We wait.” (\textbf{Esperamos.}) Does Portuguese add a word matching English “for” in \textbf{Espero o meu irmão}? (\textbf{No.}) Next, the same verb will take one carefully separated new meaning.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[espero que sim]{espero que sim — I hope so}

\label{lesson:PT-C21-esperar-hope}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Espero} first meant “I hope.” Learn that meaning in one useful answer: \textbf{Espero que sim}, “I hope so.”
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Bank the whole answer}
\begin{quote}
— Vai chover? — Is it going to rain? — \textbf{Espero que sim.} — I hope so.
\end{quote}

You do not need to take the answer apart yet. Hear and say the four beats: \textbf{es-pe-ro que sim}.

The earlier meaning, “wait,” is still available. The sentence around \textbf{esperar} selects the meaning.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} “I hope so” — \textbf{Espero que sim.}
  \item \emph{Choose:} In \textbf{Espero que sim}, does \textbf{espero} mean wait or hope? (\textbf{Hope.})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say “I hope so.” (\textbf{Espero que sim.}) Which meaning came first in the word’s Latin history? (\textbf{Hope.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[esperar]{esperar — to expect}

\label{lesson:PT-C21-esperar-expect}



\begin{quote}
You have used \textbf{esperar} for waiting and hoping. Its third common meaning gets its own short lesson: “to expect.”
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Let the object choose the meaning}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Espero um livro.} — I expect a book.
\end{quote}

Here \textbf{espero} is about what you think will arrive. Compare the three meanings:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Espero o meu irmão.} — I wait for my brother.
  \item \textbf{Espero que sim.} — I hope so.
  \item \textbf{Espero um livro.} — I expect a book.
\end{itemize}

Do not memorise three new verbs. Notice how the rest of the sentence guides you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} “I expect a book” — \textbf{Espero um livro.}
  \item \emph{Choose:} In that sentence, wait, hope or expect? (\textbf{Expect.})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say “I expect a book.” (\textbf{Espero um livro.}) What helps you choose the English meaning? (\textbf{The rest of the sentence.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[comprar]{comprar — buying, and a Latin twin that is not a twin}

\label{lesson:PT-C21-comprar}



\begin{quote}
The last verb of the chapter is the easiest to conjugate and hides the sharpest piece of etymology in it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: A plain -ar verb, and a past you already own}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{compro} & nós \textbf{compramos} \\
tu \textbf{compras} & vocês/eles \textbf{compram} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{compra} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Compro o pão.} — \textquotedblleft{}I buy the bread.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Tenho comprado pão.} — \textquotedblleft{}I have been buying bread lately.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

That second one is the trap English speakers walk into. \emph{Tenho comprado} does \textbf{not} mean \textquotedblleft{}I have bought.\textquotedblright{} It means the buying has gone on, repeatedly, over recent time. For the plain finished past, Portuguese uses \textbf{comprei}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{comprar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{comparāre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to procure, to get ready, to obtain\textquotedblright{} — \emph{com-} plus \emph{\textbf{parāre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to make ready.\textquotedblright{} Buying is procuring.

Here is the sharp part. Latin had a \textbf{second} \emph{comparāre}, spelled letter for letter the same, built instead on \emph{pār}, \textquotedblleft{}equal\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}to set side by side, to match.\textquotedblright{} That one is where English \textbf{compare} comes from. So \emph{comprar} and \emph{compare} look like an obvious pair and are not related at all: same spelling in Latin, two different parents.

The real cousins of \emph{comprar} are the \emph{parāre} family: \textbf{prepare} (\emph{prae-}, beforehand), \textbf{repair} (\emph{re-}, made ready anew), \textbf{separate} (\emph{sē-}, ready apart), \textbf{apparatus} — and even \textbf{emperor}, from \emph{imperāre}.

Note what Portuguese did to the word on the way: \emph{comparāre} lost a whole syllable to become \emph{comprar}. It wore \emph{annus} down too, dropping one of its two \emph{n}'s to give \textbf{ano}, where Spanish instead pushed them together into \emph{año}.

And the \emph{com-} of \emph{comprar} is the same \emph{com-} as in \textbf{compreender}, from \emph{comprehendere}, \textquotedblleft{}to seize together.\textquotedblright{} One prefix, two very different grips.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole chapter, first person — \textquotedblleft{}trago, consigo, espero, compro\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Compro o pão\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Tenho comprado pão\textquotedblright{}
  \item holding your years — \textquotedblleft{}Tenho vinte anos\textquotedblright{}
  \item the ready family — \textquotedblleft{}prepare · repair · separate\textquotedblright{}
  \item one prefix, two grips — \textquotedblleft{}comprar · compreender\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the chapter's four verbs in the \emph{eu} form. (\textbf{Trago, consigo, espero, compro}.) Does \emph{tenho comprado} mean \textquotedblleft{}I have bought\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No} — \textquotedblleft{}I have been buying, lately\textquotedblright{}; the finished past is \emph{comprei}.) Is \emph{comprar} related to English \emph{compare}? (\textbf{No} — two Latin verbs spelled alike; \emph{comprar} is the one from \emph{parāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to make ready,\textquotedblright{} which also gave \emph{prepare} and \emph{repair}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I am twenty.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Tenho vinte anos}} — Portuguese \textbf{holds} its years.) Which verb means \textquotedblleft{}to seize together\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Compreender}}, from \emph{comprehendere}.) And the three jobs of \emph{esperar}? (\textbf{Wait}, \textbf{hope}, \textbf{expect}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
